newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thailand extends suspension of 16 finance firms.
newsitem.headline: Thailand extends suspension of 16 finance firms.

text.p: The Thai finance ministry on Friday said it would suspend the lending and deposit taking business of 16 cash-strapped finance firms for a further nine to 12 months after an initial freeze on their operations.

A ministry statement said the extended suspension was needed to allow the firms to consolidate through mergers with other stronger local and foreign institutions, following a one-month freeze that ended this week.
The 16 firms, with estimated combined assets of 400 billion baht ($12.5 billion) at the end of the first quarter, had been ordered to stop doing business since late June.
During the extended suspension, the 16 troubled companies could not take new public deposits, and clients holding promissary notes issued by them could not withdraw their savings, the ministry said.
They could, however, exchange the notes for new, longer maturity papers issued by Krungthai Thanakit Plc, a unit of state-owned Krung Thai Bank Plc.
It said local and foreign creditors, including those holding bills of exchange and negotiable certificates of deposits issued by the suspended firms, would be treated fairly and equally.

During the suspended period, the firms could recall outstanding loans from their debtors, and those that also operated securities business can continue handling stock transactions for their clients, the statement said.

The finance companies are among Thailand's 91 non-bank financial institutions that have faced a severe liquidity crunch for more than a year due mainly to their over-exposure to the ailing property sector.

Niphat Pukkanasutr, head of a government-appointed bailout committee, told reporters on Friday the latest measures for the 16 firms were in line with suggestions made by officials of the International Monetary Fund (IMF).

"The measures reflect proposals made by the IMF, which has experience in tackling similar problems in Mexico... I think they are on the right track in restoring public confidence," Niphat told a press conference.

The finance ministry said two of the troubled firms had agreed to merge with Krungthai Thanakit while another two had submitted plans to merge with one of five major and healthy private finance firms nominated by the government.
It said the remaining 12 firms had informed the authorities of their plans to raise capital by finding new partners. It did not identify the companies.
The central bank said earlier that as a bailout incentive, Thailand would waive its 25 percent foreign ownership limit currently imposed on Thai financial institutions.
Development Bank of Singapore said early this month it had agreed to raise, to 60 percent from 9.5 percent, its stake in Sri Dhana Finance Plc, one of the 16 suspended firms.

The ministry statement said independent or government- appointed auditors would spend the next two months reviewing assets and liabilities of any suspended finance firms still failing to produce merger plans.
It said the firms would need to negotiate debt restructuring with their local and foreign creditors that may involve turning part of their debts into equitie.
